name: Boeing 737-800
numberBuilt: 7,124 737 Next Generation aircraft of all models
summary: The 737-800 is the most popular member of Boeing's 737 Next Generation family, a single-aisle jet built for flights of a few hours. It has been the backbone of Australian domestic flying for over 20 years, so it is one of the aeroplanes you are most likely to fly on between Melbourne and Sydney, Brisbane or Perth.
funFacts: More than 7,000 737 Next Generation jets were built, and the 737-800 is by far the most common version.
The RAAF's P-8A Poseidon submarine-hunting aircraft is a military version of the 737-800, packed with sensors instead of passenger seats.
The 737 sits so low to the ground that its engines have slightly flattened bottoms so they do not scrape the runway.
Boeing stopped building passenger 737-800s in 2020, but military versions are still being made.
spotterTips: Look for two engines with flattened lower lips tucked close under the wings, and tall upturned winglets on most aircraft. It is longer than the A320 and its nose is more pointed, with a cockpit window line that dips at the corners.

melbourne.where: Seen all day at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on domestic and short international flights. You can also watch them from the Melbourne Airport viewing areas off Sharps Road.
melbourne.operators: Qantas, Virgin Australia

name: Boeing 737 MAX 8
numberBuilt: 2,483 737 MAX aircraft of all models (by September 2026)
summary: The 737 MAX 8 is the newest version of the Boeing 737, with bigger, more efficient engines and redesigned wingtips. It carries about the same number of people as the 737-800 but uses less fuel and can fly further.
funFacts: The 737 MAX was grounded around the world for about 20 months from March 2019 while Boeing fixed a problem with its flight control software.
Its LEAP-1B engines are so large that Boeing had to make the nose landing gear taller and move the engines further forward on the wing.
The MAX has split-tip winglets that point both up and down, which help it use less fuel.
More than 4,800 737 MAX jets were still waiting to be built and delivered in late 2026.
spotterTips: The easiest clues are the split winglets that point both up and down, and the zig-zag (sawtooth) edges at the back of the engine covers. The engines are rounder and sit further forward than on a 737-800.

melbourne.where: Regularly flies in and out of Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on domestic and short international routes.
melbourne.operators: Virgin Australia

photo.file: Virgin Australia (VH-8VB) Boeing 737 MAX 8 at Melbourne Airport, Oct 2025.jpg

name: Airbus A320
engines: 2 × CFM International CFM56-5B or IAE V2500 turbofans
summary: The A320 is a single-aisle airliner and the main member of the A320 family, the best-selling airliner family in the world. It was the first airliner to use digital fly-by-wire controls, meaning the pilots' inputs go to computers that then move the control surfaces.
funFacts: Instead of a big control wheel, A320 pilots fly with a small sidestick beside their seat, a bit like a gaming joystick.
The A320 family overtook the Boeing 737 as the best-selling airliner family in 2019.
Around 12,900 A320 family jets have been built, which works out to more than one new jet rolling out every day for decades.
Newer A320s have upturned wingtips called sharklets, while older ones have small fences that point both up and down.
spotterTips: Compared with a 737, the A320 has a rounder, blunter nose, a cockpit window line that is straight across, and round engines hanging lower below the wing. Older ones have small triangular wingtip fences, newer ones have tall curved sharklets.

melbourne.where: Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) is the home base of Jetstar, so A320s are everywhere there. You may also see them at Avalon Airport.
melbourne.operators: Jetstar, plus visiting Asian airlines

name: Airbus A321neo and A321XLR
nickname: XLR (for the extra long range version)
specsVariant: A321neo (97 t version); the A321XLR can fly up to about 8,700 km
engines: 2 × CFM LEAP-1A or Pratt & Whitney PW1100G geared turbofans
summary: The A321neo is the longest member of the A320 family, fitted with new fuel-saving engines (neo stands for new engine option). The A321XLR version carries extra fuel so a single-aisle jet can fly routes that once needed a big wide-body, such as Australia to parts of Asia.
funFacts: The A321XLR first flew on 15 June 2022 from Hamburg, Germany.
The XLR has an extra fuel tank built into the rear of its belly, letting it fly about 4,700 nautical miles (about 8,700 km).
The A321neo entered service on 31 May 2017 with Virgin America in the United States.
Qantas chose the A321XLR to replace its Boeing 737-800s on many routes.
spotterTips: It looks like a stretched A320 with big round engines and sharklet wingtips. Count the doors: the A321 has extra exits over or near the wing, and its body looks noticeably long and thin.

melbourne.where: Common at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on domestic and trans-Tasman flights.
melbourne.operators: Jetstar (A321neo), Qantas (A321XLR)

name: Airbus A330
engines: 2 × General Electric CF6, Pratt & Whitney PW4000 or Rolls-Royce Trent 700 turbofans
summary: The A330 is a twin-engine wide-body jet with two aisles, used for flights across Australia and to Asia and the Pacific. It shares its wing with the four-engine A340 and its cockpit with the A320, which made it easy for airlines to train pilots on several Airbus types.
funFacts: The RAAF's KC-30A air-to-air refuelling tankers are military versions of the A330-200.
The A330 and the four-engine A340 were developed together and use the same wing.
Customers could choose from three different engine makers for the original A330.
More than 1,600 A330s have been built since it first flew in 1992.
spotterTips: Look for a big twin-engine jet with two aisles' worth of fuselage, small upturned winglets and a rounded Airbus nose. Its main landing gear has four wheels on each leg, which helps tell it apart from the six-wheel 777.

melbourne.where: Seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on flights to Perth and Asia. RAAF KC-30A tankers based on the A330 often appear at the Avalon Airshow.
melbourne.operators: Qantas, several Asian airlines, RAAF (KC-30A)

photo.file: Qantas Airbus A330-300 (VH-QPJ) on finals into Brisbane Airport.jpg

name: Airbus A330neo
summary: The A330neo is an updated A330 with new Rolls-Royce engines and a longer wing, so it burns less fuel and can fly further. It entered service in December 2018 with TAP Air Portugal.
funFacts: The Trent 7000 is the only engine available for the A330neo, so every one is powered by Rolls-Royce.
Its wingspan grew to 64 m thanks to new curved sharklet wingtips, about 3.7 m wider than the original A330.
There are two models, the A330-800 and the larger A330-900, and the -900 is much more popular.
neo stands for new engine option.
spotterTips: It looks like an A330 but with large, curved sharklet wingtips instead of small winglets, and bigger engines with a different shape. Many also have the cockpit windows outlined in black, like the A350.

melbourne.where: Occasionally seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on flights from Asia and the Pacific.
melbourne.operators: Visiting international airlines

name: Boeing 787 Dreamliner
engines: 2 × General Electric GEnx-1B or Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 turbofans
summary: The 787 Dreamliner was the first airliner with most of its body and wings made from carbon fibre composite instead of aluminium. That makes it light and efficient enough to fly very long routes, such as non-stop from Australia to Europe.
funFacts: On 25 March 2018 a Qantas 787-9 flew the first scheduled non-stop flight from Australia to the UK, from Perth to London in about 17 hours.
Instead of window shades, the 787 has electronic windows that passengers dim with a button.
Its wings bend upwards a lot in flight, which is normal and makes the wingtips look like they are curving towards the sky.
The back edges of the engine covers have zig-zag chevrons that help make the engines quieter.
spotterTips: Look for long, very flexible wings that curve up at the tips with no winglets (raked wingtips), zig-zag edges on the engine covers, and a smooth, rounded nose with four cockpit windows.

melbourne.where: A daily sight at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on long-haul flights to North America, Asia, the Middle East and New Zealand.
melbourne.operators: Qantas, Air New Zealand, United Airlines, plus many visiting airlines

photo.file: Qantas - VH-ZNF - Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner - QF6027 - VGHS.jpg

name: Airbus A350
summary: The A350 is Airbus's newest long-range wide-body jet, built largely from carbon fibre composites like the Boeing 787. It is quiet, efficient and can fly some of the longest routes in the world.
funFacts: In July 2026 an A350-1000ULR test aircraft built for Qantas flew non-stop from Toulouse in France to Melbourne in about 19 hours and 12 minutes.
Qantas ordered 12 A350-1000s for Project Sunrise, its plan for non-stop flights from Sydney to London and New York.
The black mask painted around the cockpit windows is a design feature that makes it look a bit like a raccoon.
Every A350 is powered by Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines, the only engine offered for it.
spotterTips: The dark mask around the cockpit windows is the giveaway. It also has wingtips that curve smoothly upwards and two large engines with no zig-zag edges.

melbourne.where: Seen daily at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on flights to Asia and the Middle East.
melbourne.operators: Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Qatar Airways and other international airlines

photo.artist: 馬鱈作定 | バタラサクティ

name: Airbus A380
engines: 4 × Rolls-Royce Trent 900 or Engine Alliance GP7200 turbofans
summary: The A380 is the largest passenger airliner ever built, with two full decks running the whole length of the aeroplane. It is so big that airports had to build special gates with extra air bridges to load both decks.
funFacts: Its wings are about 79.75 m from tip to tip and cover 845 square metres, bigger than three tennis courts.
Emirates is by far the biggest A380 operator, with more than 100 of them.
Only 251 A380s were delivered to airlines before production ended.
The tail is 24 m tall, about the height of an eight-storey building.
spotterTips: Two full rows of windows from nose to tail, four engines and a huge, thick wing make it unmistakable. The nose has a rounded, bulbous shape with the cockpit tucked between the two decks.

melbourne.where: Seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on long-haul flights, especially to Dubai. Its size makes it easy to spot even from a distance.
melbourne.operators: Emirates, Qantas

photo.file: Qantas a380 vh-oqa takeoff heathrow arp.jpg

name: Boeing 777
summary: The 777 is the world's largest twin-engine airliner family in service and one of the most successful long-haul jets ever. The 777-300ER can carry nearly as many people as a 747 with only two engines.
funFacts: The GE90-115B engines on the 777-300ER are among the most powerful jet engines ever built, each producing about 115,000 pounds of thrust.
The 777 was the first Boeing airliner designed entirely on computers.
Each main landing gear leg has six wheels, so a 777 lands on twelve main wheels plus two at the nose.
The 777 entered service with United Airlines on 7 June 1995.
spotterTips: Look for two enormous engines, a long body and six-wheel main landing gear. The tail cone at the back ends in a sharp, flat blade shape instead of a rounded point.

melbourne.where: Seen daily at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on long-haul flights to the Middle East, Asia and beyond.
melbourne.operators: Emirates, Qatar Airways and other international airlines

name: Boeing 747
nickname: Jumbo Jet, Queen of the Skies
summary: The 747 was the original Jumbo Jet, the first wide-body airliner, and it made long-distance flying affordable for millions of people. Production ended in 2023 after more than 50 years, and today most 747s still flying carry cargo.
funFacts: In 1991 an El Al 747 carried 1,087 passengers in a single flight during Operation Solomon, an airlift from Ethiopia to Israel.
The famous hump was designed so the nose could swing open for loading cargo, with the cockpit moved up out of the way.
The 747 was the first airliner to use an inertial navigation system, so it did not need a navigator in the cockpit.
Its maximum takeoff weight grew from about 333 tonnes on the 747-100 to about 440 tonnes on the 747-8.
spotterTips: The hump at the front of the upper deck is the giveaway, plus four engines under the wings. The 747-400 and 747-8 also have upturned or raked wingtips.

melbourne.where: Mostly seen as cargo freighters at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine), often at night or early morning. Qantas retired its last passenger 747 in 2020.
melbourne.operators: International cargo airlines

photo.file: Landing of Boeing 747-400 of Qantas at Brisbane Airport.jpg

name: Boeing 777X
summary: The 777X is the next generation of the Boeing 777, with new carbon fibre wings and the GE9X, the largest jet engine ever built. The 777-9 will be the longest airliner ever, and it is due to start carrying passengers in 2027.
funFacts: Its wingtips fold upwards on the ground so it can fit into the same airport gates as a normal 777.
At 76.73 m long, the 777-9 is longer than both the 747-8 and the A380.
The 777-9 first flew on 25 January 2020, but certification delays have pushed its first deliveries back several years.
The fan at the front of each GE9X engine is about 3.4 m across, almost as wide as the body of a Boeing 737.
spotterTips: Look for the hinge line near each wingtip where the folding tips sit, and huge engines on a very long body. It has raked, pointed wingtips with no winglets.

photo.artist: Dan Nevill from Seattle, WA, United States

name: COMAC C919
summary: The C919 is China's first large home-grown jet airliner, designed to compete with the Airbus A320 and Boeing 737. It carried its first paying passengers on 28 May 2023 with China Eastern Airlines.
funFacts: Although it is Chinese-designed, its LEAP-1C engines come from CFM International, a joint company of GE (United States) and Safran (France).
It is almost exactly the same size as an A320, with a wingspan of 35.8 m.
COMAC has planned longer and shorter versions as well as an extended-range model.
spotterTips: It looks very similar to an A320, with round engines under the wings and upturned winglets. The COMAC name and Chinese airline colours are the best clues.

name: Airbus A220
summary: The A220 was designed in Canada by Bombardier as the CSeries and became an Airbus in 2018. It is a modern, quiet jet sized between regional planes and the A320, and QantasLink flies it from Melbourne.
funFacts: QantasLink began A220 passenger flights on 1 March 2024, flying from Melbourne to Canberra and Brisbane.
QantasLink's first A220 was painted in an Aboriginal art livery called Minyma Kutjara Tjukurpa.
Its geared turbofan engines have a gearbox so the big fan can spin slower than the engine core, which saves fuel and reduces noise.
The economy cabin has a 2-3 layout, so only one side has a middle seat.
spotterTips: Look for a slim jet with very large engines for its size, big rectangular-ish windows and a small curved winglet. The nose is short and rounded.

melbourne.where: Seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on QantasLink domestic flights.
melbourne.operators: QantasLink

photo.file: 20250407 Airbus A220-300 of QantasLink (VH-X4D) at HBA.jpg

name: Embraer E190
summary: The E190 is a Brazilian regional jet from the E-Jet family, built for routes that are too busy for a turboprop but too small for a 737 or A320. Australia's Alliance Airlines is the world's largest E190 operator.
funFacts: Alliance Airlines operates 64 E190s, more than any other airline in the world.
E-Jets have a double-bubble shaped body with a 2-2 seat layout, so there are no middle seats.
Embraer is based in Brazil and is the third-largest maker of airliners after Airbus and Boeing.
The newer E190-E2 version has bigger geared turbofan engines and a longer wing.
spotterTips: Look for a small twin jet with engines under the wings, a long slender nose and a low-slung body. It is shorter than a 737 and its tail fin is tall and slightly swept.

melbourne.where: Seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on regional and charter flights, sometimes flying on behalf of the major airlines.
melbourne.operators: Alliance Airlines

name: Fokker 100
summary: The Fokker 100 is a Dutch-built regional jet with its two engines mounted at the back and a T-shaped tail. Fokker stopped making aircraft in the 1990s, but Australia became one of the last strongholds of the type, flying workers to mines in remote areas.
funFacts: Production ended in 1997 after Fokker went bankrupt, so every Fokker 100 flying today is at least 28 years old.
Qantas donated retired Fokker 100s to the Historical Aircraft Restoration Society museum at Parkes in New South Wales.
Australian operators used the type heavily for fly-in fly-out mining flights.
spotterTips: Two engines mounted on the rear fuselage beside a tall T-tail, with a clean wing that has no engines under it. It looks a bit like a smaller, sleeker DC-9.

melbourne.where: Occasionally seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on charter flights.
melbourne.operators: Alliance Airlines

name: De Havilland Canada Dash 8 Q400
summary: The Q400 is the largest and fastest member of the Dash 8 family of propeller-driven regional airliners. It links smaller cities to the big airports and is almost as quick as a jet on short routes.
funFacts: The Q stands for quiet, because these aircraft have a system that reduces noise and vibration in the cabin.
With a high-speed cruise of up to about 667 km/h, the Q400 is one of the fastest turboprop airliners flying.
Production of the Dash 8 has been paused since 2022 while De Havilland Canada plans a new factory.
spotterTips: A high wing with two big engines, each spinning a six-blade propeller, and a T-tail. The main landing gear folds into the engine pods and the body is long and slim.

melbourne.where: Seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on regional flights to other cities in Victoria, New South Wales and Tasmania.
melbourne.operators: QantasLink

photo.file: QantasLink Bombardier Dash 8-Q400 VH-QOR Sydney Airport.jpg

name: Saab 340
summary: The Saab 340 is a small Swedish turboprop airliner with 34 seats, built for short regional hops. In Australia it is the workhorse of Rex (Regional Express), linking country towns with the capital cities.
funFacts: It was designed by Saab, the Swedish company that also builds the Gripen fighter jet.
The project started as a partnership with Fairchild in the United States, which is why early ones were called the SF340.
Rex in Australia has been one of the biggest Saab 340 operators in the world.
spotterTips: A small, low-wing turboprop with two engines and four-blade propellers, a pointed nose and a tall, swept tail fin.

melbourne.where: Seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on regional flights to country towns in Victoria, New South Wales, Tasmania and King Island.
melbourne.operators: Rex (Regional Express)

name: ATR 72
summary: The ATR 72 is a twin turboprop airliner built by a French and Italian partnership. It is one of the most popular regional aircraft in the world because it is cheap to run on short routes.
funFacts: ATR is a joint company owned by Airbus and the Italian firm Leonardo.
Passengers usually board through a door at the back, while cargo goes in a door at the front.
It first entered service with Finnair in 1989.
The latest ATR 72-600 can carry up to 72 passengers, which is where the name comes from.
spotterTips: A high wing mounted on top of the body, two engines with six-blade propellers, a T-tail, and main landing gear that folds into bulges on the sides of the body rather than into the engines.

name: De Havilland Canada Twin Otter
manufacturer: De Havilland Canada (also built by Viking Air)
role: Short takeoff and landing (STOL) utility aircraft
summary: The Twin Otter is a rugged small turboprop that can take off and land on very short, rough strips, snow or water. It is used everywhere from Antarctic research bases to tropical island hops.
funFacts: It can be fitted with wheels, skis or floats, so it can operate from runways, snow and ice, or lakes and the sea.
Production stopped in 1988 but was restarted by Viking Air, and the 1,000th Twin Otter was delivered in 2026.
Its fixed landing gear never retracts, which keeps it simple and tough for rough strips.
spotterTips: A boxy body, a high straight wing braced by struts, two engines on the wing and fixed landing gear with a nose wheel. It looks a bit like a flying minibus.

photo.file: WinAir De Havilland Canada DHC-6-300 Twin Otter Breidenstein.jpg

name: Boeing 777 Freighter
engines: 2 × General Electric GE90-110B or GE90-115B turbofans
summary: The 777F is the cargo version of the Boeing 777, based on the long-range 777-200LR. It can carry about 100 tonnes of freight across oceans, from fresh food to cars and medicines.
funFacts: The first 777F was delivered to Air France on 19 February 2009.
It has no passenger windows, so the outside looks like a smooth tube with only a few doors.
It can fly nearly 9,200 km fully loaded, letting airlines carry cargo between continents without stopping.
A new 777-8 Freighter based on the 777X is being developed to replace it.
spotterTips: It looks like a 777, with the same six-wheel landing gear and huge engines, but has no row of windows along the body and a large cargo door on the left side behind the wing.

melbourne.where: Visits Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on international cargo flights, often at night or early morning.
melbourne.operators: International cargo airlines

photo.file: Leipzig Halle Airport Kalitta Air DHL Aviation Boeing 777-F N775CK (DSC07744).jpg

name: Airbus BelugaXL
role: Outsize cargo aircraft for carrying aircraft parts
summary: The BelugaXL is a giant cargo plane built from an Airbus A330 with a huge bubble-shaped upper body. Airbus uses it to fly big aircraft parts, such as wings and fuselage sections, between its factories in Europe.
funFacts: It can carry two A350 wings at once, while the older BelugaST could carry only one.
Its painted eyes and smile make it look like a beluga whale, and the design was picked in a vote by Airbus employees.
The cockpit sits lower than the cargo deck so the whole nose can swing up for loading.
Its bulging cargo hold is about 1.7 m wider than the older BelugaST's.
spotterTips: Impossible to miss: a huge rounded hump above a low cockpit, like a whale's head, with A330 wings and engines. Most are painted white with a whale face on the nose.

photo.file: Hamburg-Finkenwerder Airport Airbus Transport International Airbus A330-743L Beluga XL F-GXLH (DSC09365).jpg

name: Boeing Dreamlifter
role: Outsize cargo aircraft for carrying 787 parts
summary: The Dreamlifter is a Boeing 747-400 rebuilt with an enormous swollen body to carry parts of the 787 Dreamliner from factories around the world to Boeing's assembly lines. The whole tail section swings open sideways so big parts can be slid straight in.
funFacts: Its cargo hold has a volume of about 1,840 cubic metres, three times as much as a normal 747 freighter.
In November 2013 a Dreamlifter landed by mistake at the small Jabara Airport in Wichita, Kansas, instead of a nearby air force base, and had to take off from the short runway.
Its swing tail was designed with help from a Spanish company, Gamesa.
The cargo section is not pressurised, so parts travel in the cold, thin air at cruising height.
spotterTips: A 747 front end and wings with a huge, fat body behind the cockpit that rises higher than the hump. Look for the hinge line near the tail where it swings open.

photo.artist: ERIC SALARD from LE GRAND VILLAGE PLAGE, FRANCE

name: Antonov An-124 Ruslan
crew: Up to 8 (pilots, navigator, flight engineers, radio operator and loadmasters)
passengers: 88 in the upper deck, plus up to 120 tonnes of cargo
summary: The An-124 is one of the biggest cargo aeroplanes in the world, able to carry loads like locomotives, mining trucks and even other aircraft. With the An-225 destroyed, it is now the largest cargo plane in regular commercial service.
funFacts: Its nose swings up and its tail has a ramp, so cargo can be driven straight through from front or back.
It has 24 wheels, and its landing gear can kneel down to lower the front of the plane to the ground for easier loading.
It can carry about 120 tonnes of cargo, roughly the weight of 80 family cars.
On a ferry flight with no cargo it can fly about 14,000 km.
spotterTips: A huge high-wing aircraft with four engines, a drooping wing, a single tall tail, and a long row of wheels under the belly. The nose has a bulging upper cockpit area above an upward-opening cargo door.

melbourne.where: Occasionally visits Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) or Avalon on special heavy-lift charter flights carrying oversized cargo.
melbourne.operators: Antonov Airlines

name: Antonov An-225 Mriya
summary: The An-225 Mriya was the heaviest aeroplane ever built and the one with the largest wingspan of any aircraft in service. Only one was ever finished, and it was destroyed at Hostomel Airport near Kyiv on 27 February 2022 during the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
funFacts: It was originally built to carry the Soviet Buran space shuttle on its back.
Its maximum takeoff weight was 640 tonnes, heavier than any other aeroplane ever flown.
In May 2016 it flew a huge electrical generator to Perth in Western Australia, and crowds gathered to watch it land.
It had six engines and 32 wheels to spread out its enormous weight.
spotterTips: Six engines under a very long high wing and a twin tail with two fins at the ends of the tailplane. It looked like a stretched An-124 with a different tail.

photo.file: Antonov Design Bureau Antonov An-225 Mriya at Leipzig Halle (EDDP-LEJ).jpg

name: Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II
summary: The F-35 is a stealth fighter, shaped and coated so it is very hard for radar to see. It can fight other aircraft, attack targets on the ground and gather information with its powerful sensors. It is now the main fighter jet of the Royal Australian Air Force.
funFacts: There are three versions: the F-35A takes off from normal runways, the F-35B can hover and land vertically, and the F-35C lands on aircraft carriers.
Each pilot's helmet costs about US$400,000 and lets them look through the floor of the aircraft using cameras mounted around the jet.
Australia ordered 72 F-35As, and all of them had been delivered by the end of 2024.
Although its official name is Lightning II, many pilots call it the Panther.
spotterTips: Look for a chunky single-engine jet with two angled tail fins, a diamond-shaped nose and no missiles hanging under the wings, because it carries weapons inside to stay stealthy. It is much louder than most other jets at airshows.

melbourne.where: Watch for F-35As at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong (next held in 2027), where the RAAF has flown it in displays, and on flypasts for big events such as Anzac Day.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 2 Operational Conversion Unit and No. 3 and No. 77 Squadrons at RAAF Base Williamtown, and No. 75 Squadron at RAAF Base Tindal)

photo.artist: U.S. Air Force photo by Master Sgt. Donald R. Allen

name: Boeing F/A-18F Super Hornet
summary: The Super Hornet is a big, powerful twin-engine fighter built to fly from aircraft carriers. The F model has two seats, one for the pilot and one for a weapons officer who runs the sensors. Australia bought 24 of them in 2007 to replace its old F-111 bombers.
funFacts: US Navy crews call it the Rhino, partly because of a bump on top of its nose that holds an antenna.
It can carry an extra fuel tank with a hose and act as a flying fuel station to refuel other jets.
Even though it is bigger than the original Hornet, it has 42 per cent fewer structural parts.
The RAAF's first Super Hornets arrived at RAAF Base Amberley in Queensland on 26 March 2010.
spotterTips: Look for a large twin-engine jet with two tail fins that lean outwards and rectangular engine intakes under the wings. The F model has a long two-seat bubble canopy.

melbourne.where: RAAF Super Hornets have flown thrilling handling displays at the Australian Grand Prix at Albert Park and appeared at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong (next held in 2027), including air-to-air refuelling demonstrations.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 1 Squadron, RAAF Base Amberley, Queensland)

name: Boeing EA-18G Growler
summary: The Growler is a Super Hornet turned into a flying electronic jammer. Instead of a gun it carries special pods that detect enemy radars and fill them with electronic noise, so other aircraft can fly safely. Australia is the only country apart from the United States to fly it.
funFacts: It shares more than 90 per cent of its parts with the Super Hornet, but the cannon was removed to make room for electronics.
Its wingtip missile rails were swapped for pods that listen for enemy radar signals.
Two crew members do the job that needed four people in the older EA-6B Prowler.
The RAAF's first Growlers made their public debut at the 2017 Avalon Airshow.
spotterTips: It looks almost exactly like a two-seat Super Hornet, so look for the bulky pods on the wingtips and large jamming pods hanging under the wings and body.

melbourne.where: The RAAF's first two Growlers flew in for their public debut at the 2017 Avalon Airshow near Geelong. Look for them at future Avalon Airshows (next held in 2027).
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 6 Squadron, RAAF Base Amberley, Queensland)

photo.file: U.S. Navy EA-18G Growler breaks away from a U.S. Air Force KC-135 (altered).jpg

name: Boeing C-17 Globemaster III
summary: The C-17 is a giant military cargo plane that can carry tanks, helicopters and huge loads across the world, then land on short or rough runways. The RAAF uses its C-17s for everything from moving troops to delivering help after floods and bushfires.
funFacts: Crews nicknamed it The Moose because of the honking noise its fuel tank vents make during refuelling.
It can carry a 69-tonne M1 Abrams tank inside its cargo hold.
C-17s fly to Antarctica each summer, taking about five hours each way between New Zealand and McMurdo Station.
In August 2021 one C-17 carried 823 people out of Kabul in a single flight, a record for the type.
spotterTips: Look for a huge grey four-engine jet with wings mounted on top of the body, drooping wingtips with small winglets, and a tall T-shaped tail.

melbourne.where: RAAF C-17s have done low flypasts at the Australian Grand Prix at Albert Park and have flown over Melbourne, Port Phillip Bay and Geelong ahead of the Avalon Airshow (next held in 2027).
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 36 Squadron, RAAF Base Amberley, Queensland)

name: Lockheed Martin C-130J Super Hercules
summary: The Super Hercules is the modern version of the famous Hercules, a tough four-propeller transport that can land on short dirt strips. It carries troops, vehicles and supplies, and drops paratroopers and aid by parachute. Australia flies the stretched C-130J-30 model.
funFacts: Each propeller has six curved blades, compared with four on older Hercules.
The more powerful engines and propellers changed how the wing stalled, so engineers added a stick pusher system and testing was delayed by nine months.
The stretched C-130J-30 is 4.6 metres longer and can carry 92 paratroopers.
Australia ordered 20 more C-130J-30s in July 2023.
spotterTips: Look for a high-wing transport with four propeller engines, each with six scimitar-shaped blades, and an upswept tail with a loading ramp underneath.

melbourne.where: RAAF C-130Js have flown over Melbourne, Port Phillip Bay and Geelong to promote the Avalon Airshow, and often appear at the show itself (next held in 2027).
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 37 Squadron, RAAF Base Richmond, New South Wales)

photo.file: C-130J 135th AS Maryland ANG in flight.jpg

name: Airbus KC-30A (A330 MRTT)
summary: The KC-30A is an Airbus A330 airliner turned into a flying petrol station. It can pass fuel to fighter jets and other aircraft in mid-air, so they can fly much further. It can also carry passengers and cargo at the same time.
funFacts: The RAAF received the first A330 tanker delivered to any customer, handed over at RAAF Base Amberley on 1 June 2011.
It can refuel aircraft two ways: with a long boom under the tail, or with hoses that trail from pods under each wing.
The refuelling operator sits in the cockpit and watches the refuelling on 2D and 3D screens.
One RAAF KC-30A has a VIP fit-out and has flown the Prime Minister overseas.
spotterTips: It looks like an A330 airliner in military grey, but look for the refuelling boom under the tail and the hose pods hanging under each wing.

melbourne.where: KC-30As have performed air-to-air refuelling demonstrations with fighter jets at the Avalon Airshow (next held in 2027) and took part in the 2014 Centenary of Military Aviation air show at RAAF Williams, Point Cook.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 33 Squadron, RAAF Base Amberley, Queensland)

photo.artist: U.S. Air Force photo by Christian Turner
photo.file: KC-30 A39-002 refuelling an USAF F-16 (cropped).jpg

name: Boeing P-8A Poseidon
summary: The P-8A Poseidon is a Boeing 737 airliner rebuilt to hunt submarines and keep watch over the ocean. It searches huge areas of sea for ships and submarines, and also helps with search and rescue. Australia guards a very long coastline, so these aircraft are very important to the RAAF.
funFacts: It is based on the Boeing 737-800, the same type of airliner many people fly on holidays.
It drops sonobuoys, small floating listening devices that hear submarines underwater and radio the sounds back to the aircraft.
It works together with the MQ-4C Triton, a large robot aircraft that flies very long surveillance missions.
The RAAF has 14 P-8As, with the last one delivered in May 2026.
spotterTips: It looks like a grey Boeing 737, but has no passenger windows along most of the body, raked wingtips with no winglets, and lots of antennas on the belly.

melbourne.where: A P-8A from No. 11 Squadron flew at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong in 2025. Look for it again at the next show in 2027.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 11, No. 12 and No. 292 Squadrons, RAAF Base Edinburgh, South Australia)

photo.file: RAAF (A47-001) Boeing P-8A Poseidon aerial display at the RAAF Base Richmond Air Show 2025.jpg

name: Boeing E-7A Wedgetail
role: Airborne early warning and control aircraft
summary: The Wedgetail is a flying radar station built from a Boeing 737. Its big radar can watch the sky and sea for hundreds of kilometres in every direction, and its crew directs friendly aircraft like air traffic controllers in the sky. It was developed for Australia first, and now other air forces are buying it too.
funFacts: It is named after the wedge-tailed eagle, Australia's largest bird of prey.
The radar does not spin like older radar dishes. It steers its beam electronically instead.
The flat radar on its back is nicknamed the top hat.
Australia has six, all flown by No. 2 Squadron.
spotterTips: Look for a grey Boeing 737 with a long, flat, blade-like radar mounted on top of the body, plus small fins under the tail.

melbourne.where: An E-7A was on static display at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong in 2025, where visitors could see it up close. Look for it again at the next show in 2027.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 2 Squadron, RAAF Base Williamtown, New South Wales)

photo.artist: US Air Force photo by Richard Gonzales
photo.file: A30-001 in flight over the United States in April 2025 (cropped).jpg

name: Pilatus PC-21
summary: The PC-21 is the aircraft every new RAAF pilot learns to fly on. It has a propeller, but it is so fast and agile, with a cockpit like a modern fighter, that students can learn many jet skills in it. It is also flown by the Roulettes, the RAAF's aerobatic display team.
funFacts: Pilatus says it can match speeds and climb rates that used to need a jet trainer.
Australia ordered 49 PC-21s in 2015, and all were delivered by November 2019.
The Roulettes fly seven PC-21s, including one spare.
Its cockpit screens can pretend to show radar and weapons, so students practise fighter skills without real ones.
spotterTips: Look for a sleek single-propeller aircraft with a five-bladed propeller, a long bubble canopy with two seats one behind the other, and a fighter-like shape. The Roulettes' aircraft are painted red, white and blue.

melbourne.where: Your best chance in Victoria. PC-21s are based at RAAF Base East Sale in Gippsland, home of the Roulettes and pilot training. The Roulettes perform at the Australian Grand Prix at Albert Park and at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong (next held in 2027).
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (Central Flying School and the Roulettes at RAAF Base East Sale, Victoria, and No. 2 Flying Training School at RAAF Base Pearce, Western Australia)

photo.file: Royal Australian Air Force (A54-032) Pilatus PC-21 taking off for the RAAF Roulettes display at the 2023 Australian International Airshow.jpg

name: BAE Systems Hawk 127
specsVariant: Hawk 128 (RAAF Hawk 127s have been upgraded to a similar standard)
engines: 1 × Rolls-Royce Turbomeca Adour turbofan (Mk 871 on the RAAF Hawk 127)
summary: The Hawk is a small, nimble jet trainer. After learning on the PC-21, RAAF pilots move to the Hawk to get ready for fast jets like the F-35A. It is one of the most successful jet trainers ever made.
funFacts: The famous Red Arrows display team in the United Kingdom flies Hawks.
Australia ordered 33 Hawk 127s in 1997. Twelve were built in the UK and 21 were built in Australia.
The Hawk first flew in 1974, more than 50 years ago, and is still in service.
Australian Hawks were upgraded so their cockpits work like those of modern fighters.
spotterTips: Look for a small two-seat jet with a long stepped canopy, low wings, and engine intakes on each side of the body just behind the cockpit.

melbourne.where: RAAF Hawks have appeared at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong (next held in 2027). They are based interstate, so sightings in Victoria are less common.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 76 Squadron at RAAF Base Williamtown, New South Wales, and No. 79 Squadron at RAAF Base Pearce, Western Australia)

photo.artist: Beau Giles from Newtown, Sydney, Australia

name: Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor
summary: The F-22 Raptor was the world's first stealth fighter built mainly to win battles in the air against other fighters. It combines stealth, speed and amazing agility. Only the United States Air Force flies it, because the US never allowed it to be sold overseas.
funFacts: It can supercruise, flying faster than sound at about 1,870 km/h without using its afterburners.
Its engine nozzles move up and down to push the jet around, so it can do tight, slow manoeuvres that look impossible.
Production stopped in 2011 after only 195 were built.
Australia's Chief of the Defence Force said in 2008 that Australia was interested in buying the F-22.
spotterTips: Look for a large twin-engine stealth jet with angled edges, two outward-leaning tail fins, diamond-shaped wings and flat, square engine nozzles at the back.

melbourne.where: US Air Force F-22s have flown spectacular displays at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong several times, including 2013, 2017, 2023 and 2025. The next show is in 2027.
melbourne.operators: United States Air Force (visiting)

name: Northrop B-2 Spirit
summary: The B-2 Spirit is a stealth bomber shaped like a giant boomerang. It is a flying wing with no tail at all, designed to be almost invisible to radar. Only 21 were ever built, making it one of the rarest and most expensive aircraft in the world.
funFacts: The 21 aircraft cost a total of US$44.7 billion, about US$2.13 billion each.
It has no tail fins. Computers keep it stable by moving control surfaces on the back edge of the wing.
Its wingspan of 52.4 metres is more than twice as long as its body.
All B-2s are based at Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri and live in climate-controlled hangars to protect their special coatings.
spotterTips: You cannot mistake it: a huge dark grey flying wing with no tail and a saw-tooth (zigzag) back edge.

photo.file: RAF F-35B integration flying training with USAF B-2 30092019 - 4.jpg

name: Boeing B-52 Stratofortress
crew: 5 (pilot, co-pilot, weapon systems officer, navigator and electronic warfare officer)
summary: The B-52 is a gigantic eight-engine bomber that first flew in 1952. The US Air Force has kept upgrading it for more than 70 years, and it can carry a huge load over very long distances. It is planned to keep flying until about 2050.
funFacts: If it serves until 2050 as planned, it will have been in service for about 95 years, longer than any other military aircraft type.
It has eight jet engines, hung in pairs under its long drooping wings.
The last B-52H was delivered in 1962, and those same aircraft are still flying today.
The engines are planned to be replaced, turning the B-52H into the B-52J.
spotterTips: Look for a very long, slender bomber with eight engines in four pairs under thin drooping wings, a tall tail fin, and small wheels near the wingtips.

melbourne.where: US Air Force B-52s have visited the Avalon Airshow near Geelong several times, including a static display in 2015, a visit in 2019 and a flyover in 2023. The next show is in 2027, but visits depend on US operations.
melbourne.operators: United States Air Force (visiting)

photo.file: B-52 Stratofortress assigned to the 307th Bomb Wing (cropped).jpg

name: Fairchild Republic A-10 Thunderbolt II
summary: The A-10 was built to fly low and slow to protect soldiers on the ground. It is extremely tough and was designed around an enormous cannon in its nose. It is not pretty, which is why everyone calls it the Warthog.
funFacts: The whole aircraft was designed around its huge 30 mm GAU-8 Avenger rotary cannon.
The pilot sits in a tub of titanium armour weighing about 540 kg, nicknamed the bathtub.
It is named after the P-47 Thunderbolt, a famous fighter from the Second World War.
Its retirement has been planned many times, but in April 2026 the US Air Force delayed it until 2030.
spotterTips: Look for straight, thick wings, two big round engines mounted high on the back of the body, and twin tail fins at the very end.

photo.artist: Master Sgt. William Greer, U.S. Air Force

name: General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon
summary: The F-16 is a small, light and very agile fighter, and one of the most successful jets ever made. More than 4,600 have been built and it is flown by air forces all over the world. Pilots and crews call it the Viper.
funFacts: Its first flight on 20 January 1974 was an accident. During a fast taxi test it started to wobble, so the pilot took off rather than risk crashing.
It was one of the first fighters with fly-by-wire controls, where computers help fly the plane.
The pilot's seat is tilted back 30 degrees to help cope with strong g-forces.
Its frameless bubble canopy gives the pilot a superb view in every direction.
spotterTips: Look for a small single-engine jet with one tail fin, a big air intake under the cockpit (like an open mouth) and a clear bubble canopy.

melbourne.where: F-16s have performed at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong. The Republic of Singapore Air Force Black Knights flew F-16s in 2015, and a US Air Force F-16 took part in 2025. The next show is in 2027.
melbourne.operators: Republic of Singapore Air Force and United States Air Force (visiting)

name: Eurofighter Typhoon
manufacturer: Eurofighter GmbH (Airbus, BAE Systems and Leonardo)
country: United Kingdom, Germany, Italy and Spain
summary: The Typhoon is a fast and agile fighter built by a team of four European countries working together. It was designed first to win fights against other aircraft, and later gained the ability to attack ground targets too. It is flown by several air forces in Europe and the Middle East.
funFacts: It was built jointly by the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy and Spain, with parts made in different countries.
It is deliberately unstable, so computers make thousands of tiny corrections to keep it flying smoothly.
It can reach about Mach 2.35, more than twice the speed of sound.
Its small front wings, called canards, help make it very agile.
spotterTips: Look for a triangle-shaped (delta) wing, small canard wings just behind the cockpit, a single tail fin and a large air intake under the nose.

photo.file: RAF Eurofighter EF-2000 Typhoon F2 Lofting-1.jpg

name: Dassault Rafale
summary: The Rafale is France's main fighter, able to do almost every combat job, from air defence to reconnaissance. One version can fly from France's aircraft carrier. It has become popular overseas, with hundreds more on order.
funFacts: Rafale is French for gust of wind.
The first demonstrator, the Rafale A, flew in 1986, and the production Rafale C followed in 1991.
The navy version flies from the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle.
Tests showed it could land on a carrier while still carrying heavy loads of unused weapons.
spotterTips: Look for a delta wing with small canards near the cockpit, two engines side by side, a single tail fin and curved air intakes under the wing roots.

name: Saab JAS 39 Gripen
summary: The Gripen is a small, clever Swedish fighter designed to be cheap to run and easy to look after. Sweden wanted it to be able to hide away from big airbases and operate from ordinary roads. It is flown by several countries, including Sweden, Hungary, Brazil and Thailand.
funFacts: It was designed to take off and land on stretches of public road that Sweden set up as emergency runways.
A small ground crew can refuel and rearm it quickly, even at a road base.
JAS stands for the Swedish words for fighter, attack and reconnaissance, because one aircraft does all three jobs.
A newer, bigger version called the Gripen E has a more powerful General Electric engine.
spotterTips: Look for a small single-engine jet with a delta wing, canards just behind the cockpit, and curved air intakes on each side of the body.

photo.file: Saab JAS 39 Gripen at Kaivopuisto Air Show, June 2017 (altered) copy.jpg

name: Sukhoi Su-57
summary: The Su-57 is Russia's first stealth fighter. It is large, fast and very manoeuvrable, but only a small number have been built so far. It entered service with the Russian Aerospace Forces in 2020.
funFacts: NATO countries give Russian aircraft code names, and the Su-57's is Felon.
It came from a program called PAK FA, which started in 1999.
It can supercruise at about 1,400 km/h without using afterburners.
Its engine nozzles can swivel to help it perform very tight manoeuvres.
spotterTips: Look for a long, flat stealth fighter with widely spaced engines, all-moving twin tail fins and small moving panels at the front of each wing root.

photo.file: Sukhoi Design Bureau, 054, Sukhoi T-50 (Su-57 prototype) (49581303977).jpg

name: Lockheed C-5 Galaxy
summary: The C-5 Galaxy is the biggest aircraft in the US Air Force and one of the largest military aircraft in the world. Its whole nose lifts up and its tail opens, so huge loads can drive straight through. All the remaining aircraft have been upgraded to the C-5M Super Galaxy.
funFacts: Its nose swings upwards like a giant visor so vehicles can drive in at the front.
It can kneel, lowering itself so the cargo floor is at the height of a truck tray for easy loading.
It can carry 36 cargo pallets, about 127 tonnes of cargo.
It is the largest aircraft able to fly to Antarctica, landing near McMurdo Station.
spotterTips: Look for a gigantic grey four-engine jet with wings mounted high on the body, drooping wings and a tall T-shaped tail. It is noticeably bigger than a C-17.

melbourne.where: A US Air Force C-5 Galaxy was on display at the Avalon Airshow near Geelong in 2023, and visitors could look inside. The next show is in 2027, but visiting aircraft change each time.
melbourne.operators: United States Air Force (visiting)

photo.artist: U.S. Air Force photo by Brett Snow

name: Airbus A400M Atlas
crew: 3 or 4 (2 pilots, optional third pilot and 1 loadmaster)
summary: The A400M is a big European transport aircraft that sits between the C-130 Hercules and the C-17 in size. It can carry heavy vehicles and helicopters, drop paratroopers, and even refuel other aircraft in flight. It is flown by several European air forces.
funFacts: The two propellers on each wing spin in opposite directions, which is very unusual.
Its TP400 engines are among the most powerful turboprops ever built in the West.
Before its first flight, the engine was tested by bolting it onto a C-130 Hercules.
It can carry 116 fully equipped troops or up to 37 tonnes of cargo.
spotterTips: Look for a high-wing transport with four large propellers with curved, scimitar-shaped blades, a T-tail and a big rear loading ramp.

melbourne.where: A French Air Force A400M was on static display at the 2015 Avalon Airshow near Geelong, and a German A400M visited in 2025. The next show is in 2027.
melbourne.operators: French Air and Space Force and German Air Force (visiting)

photo.file: German Air Force Airbus A400M (out cropped).jpg

name: Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey
engines: 2 × Rolls-Royce T406-AD-400 turboshafts driving tilting rotors
crew: 3 to 4 (pilot, co-pilot and 1 or 2 crew chiefs or loadmasters)
summary: The Osprey is a tiltrotor: it takes off like a helicopter, then tilts its giant rotors forward to fly like an aeroplane. This means it can land almost anywhere but travel much faster and further than a helicopter. It is mainly flown by the US Marine Corps.
funFacts: Each rotor is about 11.6 metres across, so it cannot land like a normal aeroplane with the rotors pointed forward.
For storage on ships, the wing swivels and the rotors fold so it takes up much less space.
It can carry 24 seated troops or a small vehicle inside.
US Marine Corps Ospreys spend several months a year in northern Australia as part of the Marine Rotational Force in Darwin.
spotterTips: Look for a chunky grey aircraft with a big rotor on each wingtip that can point up like a helicopter or forward like propellers, plus twin tail fins.

melbourne.where: Not often seen in Victoria. US Marine Corps MV-22B Ospreys deploy to RAAF Base Darwin each year with the Marine Rotational Force and train around northern Australia, including Townsville.
melbourne.operators: United States Marine Corps (visiting)

name: McDonnell Douglas AV-8B Harrier II
manufacturer: McDonnell Douglas and British Aerospace (now Boeing and BAE Systems)
role: Vertical or short take-off ground attack aircraft
summary: The Harrier II is a jump jet that can take off and land vertically, and even hover in mid-air like a helicopter. This lets it fly from small ships and rough clearings without a long runway. The US Marine Corps retired its Harriers in June 2026, but Spain and Italy still fly them from their ships.
funFacts: Its single engine has four swivelling nozzles that point down to hover and backwards to fly fast.
A heavily loaded Harrier usually uses a short rolling take-off, because it can lift more that way than straight up.
It mostly flies from small aircraft carriers and amphibious assault ships.
It is being replaced by the F-35B, which can also hover and land vertically.
spotterTips: Look for a small jet with wings that droop downwards, big round intakes on each side of the cockpit, and nozzles on the sides of the body instead of at the back.

photo.file: Boeing AV-8B Harrier II, Italy - Navy JP7306232.jpg

name: Grumman F-14 Tomcat
summary: The F-14 Tomcat was a big, fast US Navy fighter famous for its swing wings and its starring role in the film Top Gun. It protected aircraft carriers from attack for more than 30 years. The US Navy retired it in 2006, and today only Iran still operates a few.
funFacts: Its wings swing forward for slow flying and landing, and sweep back for high-speed flight.
The US Navy retired its last Tomcats on 22 September 2006.
It became famous after the 1986 film Top Gun, and some Navy pilots who flew it worked on the movie.
After it retired, the US stopped selling spare parts so they could not reach Iran's Tomcats.
spotterTips: Look for a large twin-tail fighter with wings that can sweep back, two widely spaced engines and a long two-seat canopy. You will most likely see one in a museum.

photo.file: US Navy 051105-F-5480T-005 An F-14D Tomcat conducts a mission over the Persian Gulf-region.jpg

name: Lockheed U-2
summary: The U-2 is a spy plane that flies so high, more than 21 kilometres up, that pilots must wear spacesuit-like pressure suits. It has huge glider-like wings and takes photos and gathers information from far above everyone else. It first flew in 1955 and the US Air Force is now slowly retiring it.
funFacts: It is so hard to land that a second U-2 pilot chases it down the runway in a fast car, calling out its height by radio.
It has wheels only under the body, so small wheels called pogos hold the wings up for take-off and simply fall off.
Its wingtips have titanium skids for when a wing touches down at the end of a landing.
It outlasted the SR-71 Blackbird, the faster jet that was meant to replace it.
spotterTips: Look for a dark grey jet with extremely long, thin, straight wings like a glider, a slim body and a single tail fin.

photo.artist: United States Department of the Air Force

name: Wright Flyer
engines: 1 × Wright 12 hp four-cylinder water-cooled piston engine turning 2 propellers
summary: The Wright Flyer was the first powered aeroplane to make a controlled, sustained flight with a pilot on board. Brothers Orville and Wilbur Wright flew it near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on 17 December 1903, and every aeroplane since then traces its story back to that day.
funFacts: Orville's first flight lasted just 12 seconds and covered about 37 metres, which is shorter than the wingspan of a Boeing 747.
The Wrights could not find a light enough car engine, so their mechanic Charlie Taylor built one from scratch.
The best flight of the day, by Wilbur, lasted 59 seconds and covered about 260 metres. Minutes later a gust of wind flipped the Flyer over and wrecked it, so it never flew again.
Small pieces of the Flyer's wood and fabric went to the Moon on Apollo 11 in 1969, and a scrap of its wing fabric flew on the Ingenuity helicopter on Mars in 2021.
spotterTips: Look for two long fabric-covered wings stacked one above the other, a small double elevator out in front of the pilot, and two propellers behind the wings. The pilot lay flat on his stomach on the lower wing.

name: Bleriot XI
role: Single-seat monoplane for sport, training and early military use
engines: 1 × Anzani 25 hp three-cylinder air-cooled piston engine
summary: The Blériot XI is the little monoplane that Louis Blériot flew across the English Channel on 25 July 1909, the first aeroplane ever to make that crossing. The flight showed the world that aeroplanes could travel between countries, and Blériot was soon flooded with orders.
funFacts: The Channel flight from Calais to Dover took about 36 minutes and won Blériot a £1,000 prize from the Daily Mail newspaper.
Blériot took off at sunrise after waiting for the wind to drop, and he had no compass for the crossing.
A Blériot XI built in 1909 and kept at the Shuttleworth Collection in England is the world's oldest airworthy aeroplane.
Its body was a box frame made from ash wood held together with wire, and much of it was left uncovered.
spotterTips: A tiny single wing mounted at the top of an open wooden box-frame body, with the propeller and small engine right at the nose. The rear of the fuselage is often bare framework with a small tail at the end.

name: Sopwith Camel
engines: 1 × Clerget 9B 130 hp nine-cylinder rotary piston engine
summary: The Sopwith Camel was a British biplane fighter of the First World War. It was tricky to fly but extremely nimble in expert hands, and pilots flying Camels were credited with more air victories than any other Allied fighter of the war.
funFacts: It was never officially called the Camel. Pilots gave it that name because of the hump-shaped metal cover over its two guns.
Its spinning rotary engine made it turn to the right very quickly but to the left more slowly, which surprised new pilots.
Pilots flying Camels were credited with downing 1,294 enemy aircraft.
Snoopy from the Peanuts comic strip imagines his doghouse is a Sopwith Camel when he battles the Red Baron.
spotterTips: A short, stubby biplane with the pilot sitting close behind the engine and a hump in front of the cockpit. The lower wing tilts upwards noticeably while the top wing is flat.

melbourne.where: Australian airmen flew Camels in the First World War. You can learn about the Australian Flying Corps, the ancestor of today's RAAF, at the RAAF Museum at Point Cook.
melbourne.operators: No. 4 Squadron, Australian Flying Corps, flew Camels on the Western Front in France.

name: Fokker Dr.I Triplane
engines: 1 × Oberursel Ur.II 110 hp nine-cylinder rotary piston engine
summary: The Fokker Dr.I was a German fighter with three wings stacked on top of each other, which made it climb fast and turn very tightly. It became world famous as the bright red aeroplane flown by Manfred von Richthofen, the Red Baron, in the First World War.
funFacts: Anthony Fokker got the idea after seeing a captured British Sopwith Triplane in 1917.
The Red Baron's final flight, in April 1918, ended in a field defended by Australian soldiers, and the Australian Flying Corps looked after his remains.
Only three original Dr.Is survived the end of the First World War, and all of them were later destroyed, so every Dr.I you see today is a replica.
The 'Dr' in its name stands for Dreidecker, which is German for triplane.
spotterTips: Three short wings stacked one above the other plus a small extra wing between the wheels. It has a square-cut tail and is often painted all red like the Red Baron's.

melbourne.where: The Red Baron was brought down in 1918 over a sector held by Australian troops in France. The Australian War Memorial in Canberra tells this story.
melbourne.operators: Flown only by the German air service. No. 3 Squadron, Australian Flying Corps, took charge of the Red Baron's remains and his triplane.

name: Vickers Vimy
role: Twin-engine biplane heavy bomber, later record-breaking long-distance aircraft
specsVariant: Vimy with Rolls-Royce Eagle VIII engines
engines: 2 × Rolls-Royce Eagle VIII V12 piston engines
summary: The Vickers Vimy was a big British biplane bomber built just as the First World War ended. It became famous for amazing long-distance flights, including the first non-stop flight across the Atlantic and the first flight from England to Australia in 1919.
funFacts: In 1919 brothers Ross and Keith Smith, with mechanics Wally Shiers and Jim Bennett, flew a Vimy from England to Darwin and won the Australian Government's £10,000 prize.
Their Vimy's registration was G-EAOU, which people joked stood for 'God 'elp all of us'.
John Alcock and Arthur Brown flew a Vimy non-stop across the Atlantic in June 1919, and their aeroplane is now in the Science Museum in London.
The Smiths' Vimy is kept in its own climate-controlled building at Adelaide Airport.
spotterTips: A large biplane with long, straight double wings, two engines mounted between the wings and a twin-rudder tail. The nose sticks out in front with an open cockpit.

melbourne.where: After reaching Darwin in December 1919, Ross and Keith Smith flew their Vimy across Australia and on to Melbourne in February 1920 to collect their prize. The aeroplane itself is now displayed at Adelaide Airport.
melbourne.operators: Ross Smith, Keith Smith, Wally Shiers and Jim Bennett.

name: Southern Cross (Fokker F.VII)
role: Three-engine monoplane used for record-breaking long-distance flights
crew: 4 on the 1928 Pacific flight (2 pilots, a navigator and a radio operator)
summary: The Southern Cross is the Fokker trimotor that Australian aviator Charles Kingsford Smith and his crew flew across the Pacific Ocean from the United States to Australia in 1928, the first flight ever to do so. It is one of the most important aeroplanes in Australian history.
funFacts: The Pacific flight in 1928 covered about 11,700 kilometres, with stops in Hawaii and Fiji before landing in Brisbane.
Before it was the Southern Cross it was the Detroiter, an Arctic exploration aeroplane that crashed in Alaska in 1926.
In September 1928 Kingsford Smith and Ulm, with a new crew, flew the Southern Cross on the first flight across the Tasman Sea from Australia to New Zealand.
A full-size flying replica was built in South Australia in the 1980s and flew again in December 2023 after restoration.
spotterTips: A high-wing monoplane with three engines, one in the nose and one hanging under each wing. The thick wooden wing sits on top of a boxy, square-sided fuselage.

melbourne.where: The real Southern Cross is in the Kingsford Smith Memorial at Brisbane Airport. A flying replica is kept by the Historical Aircraft Restoration Society at Shellharbour Airport in New South Wales.
melbourne.operators: Charles Kingsford Smith and Charles Ulm, with American crew Harry Lyon and James Warner on the Pacific flight. It was sold to the Australian Government in 1935.

photo.file: StateLibQld 1 139254 Landing the aircraft, Southern Cross in Brisbane, Queensland, ca. 1928.jpg

name: Spirit of St. Louis
engines: 1 × Wright J-5C Whirlwind 223 hp radial piston engine
summary: The Spirit of St. Louis is the single-engine aeroplane Charles Lindbergh flew alone and non-stop from New York to Paris in May 1927. The 33 and a half hour flight made Lindbergh world famous and got huge numbers of people excited about flying.
funFacts: It was designed and built in San Diego in just 60 days.
A big fuel tank sat in front of the pilot, so there was no front windscreen. Lindbergh could only see ahead by leaning out the side window or using a small periscope.
The flight covered about 5,800 kilometres and won Lindbergh the $25,000 Orteig Prize.
The original aeroplane hangs in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum in Washington, DC.
spotterTips: A silver high-wing monoplane with a single radial engine and no front window. Look for the name painted on the nose and the registration N-X-211 on the wings and tail.

name: de Havilland Tiger Moth
engines: 1 × de Havilland Gipsy Major I 130 hp four-cylinder inverted piston engine
summary: The Tiger Moth is a small British biplane that taught thousands of pilots to fly during the Second World War, including many in Australia. It is gentle in normal flying but needs real skill for aerobatics, which made it a great teacher, and many are still flying today.
funFacts: De Havilland Australia built 1,070 Tiger Moths at Bankstown in Sydney, and most of them went to the RAAF.
In 1939 and 1940 some Tiger Moths flew 'scarecrow patrols' over the sea near Britain to watch for submarines.
After the war, many Tiger Moths were turned into crop dusters and topdressers, a pioneering job for aeroplanes in New Zealand.
Some Tiger Moths were specially rebuilt in Britain for aerobatic competitions to fly better upside down.
spotterTips: A small yellow or silver biplane with two open cockpits one behind the other. The wings are swept back slightly so the pilot can climb out of the front seat easily.

melbourne.where: The RAAF Museum at Point Cook displays Tiger Moth A17-711 in wartime training colours, and the Australian National Aviation Museum at Moorabbin Airport has Tiger Moth A17-377. The RAAF's heritage squadron also flies Tiger Moth A17-692 from Point Cook.
melbourne.operators: The RAAF trained wartime pilots on Tiger Moths. Today No. 100 Squadron (Air Force Heritage Squadron) at Point Cook and private owners keep them flying.

photo.file: De Havilland (Australia) DH-82A Tiger Moth AN2319882.jpg

name: Douglas DC-3
numberBuilt: 607 airliners, and more than 16,000 including military versions such as the C-47
engines: 2 × Pratt & Whitney R-1830 Twin Wasp 14-cylinder radial piston engines
summary: The DC-3 changed air travel by making it possible for airlines to earn money just by carrying passengers. Its military version, the C-47 Dakota, carried troops and supplies all over the world in the Second World War, and some DC-3s are still flying more than 90 years after the first one.
funFacts: Counting the military versions built in the United States, the Soviet Union and Japan, more than 16,000 were made.
In 1936 KLM used DC-3s on its route from Amsterdam to Sydney, which was by far the world's longest scheduled air route at the time.
Before the DC-3, crossing the United States meant short daytime hops and overnight train journeys. A DC-3 could fly from coast to coast in about 15 to 18 hours with three stops.
Some old DC-3s have been rebuilt with modern turboprop engines and a longer body as the Basler BT-67.
spotterTips: A rounded silver twin-engine airliner that sits nose-up on the ground because it has a small tailwheel. Look for big round radial engines and a long row of square-ish windows.

melbourne.where: The Australian National Aviation Museum at Moorabbin Airport displays DC-3 VH-ANH in Ansett colours. The RAAF Museum at Point Cook also holds C-47 Dakota A65-78 in its collection.
melbourne.operators: The RAAF flew C-47 Dakotas, and Melbourne-based airlines Australian National Airways and Ansett flew DC-3s.

name: Supermarine Spitfire
summary: The Spitfire is Britain's most famous fighter aeroplane, loved for its beautiful curved wings and its role in the Battle of Britain in 1940. It kept being improved all through the Second World War, and RAAF pilots flew it in Europe and in the defence of Darwin.
funFacts: It was the only British fighter built continuously before, during and after the Second World War.
The famous oval-shaped wing was designed to be very thin for speed but still roomy enough to hold the wheels and guns.
Designer R. J. Mitchell used rivets that sat flush with the skin so the wing would be as smooth as possible.
Australian pilot Clive Caldwell is named among the notable Commonwealth Spitfire pilots of the war.
spotterTips: Look for the elliptical wings with smoothly curved tips, a long pointed nose and a bubble-shaped canopy. The Merlin engine makes a famous deep, smooth growl.

melbourne.where: The RAAF heritage squadron keeps a Spitfire Mk VIII and a Mk XVI at Temora in New South Wales, and the Mk XVI has flown at the Australian International Airshow at Avalon near Geelong.
melbourne.operators: RAAF squadrons, including No. 1 Wing RAAF which defended Darwin. Today No. 100 Squadron (Air Force Heritage Squadron) flies Spitfires.

name: North American P-51 Mustang
engines: 1 × Packard V-1650-7 Merlin V12 piston engine
summary: The P-51 Mustang was an American fighter that could fly far enough to escort bombers all the way into Germany and back. Fitted with the British Merlin engine it became one of the best fighters of the Second World War, and Australia built its own Mustangs in Melbourne.
funFacts: The first prototype was rolled out just 102 days after the order was placed.
The Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation built 200 Mustangs at Fishermans Bend in Melbourne, and the first one flew from there on 29 April 1945.
RAAF Mustangs of No. 77 Squadron later served in the Korean War.
The Mustang's range with drop tanks was more than 2,600 kilometres, which was huge for a single-seat fighter.
spotterTips: Look for the air scoop under the belly behind the wing, a bubble canopy on the P-51D, and straight wings with square-cut tips.

melbourne.where: CAC Mustangs were built at Fishermans Bend. The RAAF's heritage squadron flies CA-18 Mustang A68-170 'Duffy's Delight' from RAAF Base Point Cook, and other Australian-built Mustangs are kept airworthy at Tyabb and Morwell in Victoria.
melbourne.operators: Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation built them, and many RAAF squadrons flew them, including No. 3, 4, 76, 77, 82, 84 and 86 Squadrons.

name: CAC Boomerang
engines: 1 × Pratt & Whitney R-1830 Twin Wasp 14-cylinder radial piston engine
summary: The Boomerang was the first combat aeroplane designed and built in Australia, made in Melbourne in a hurry when Australia urgently needed fighters in 1942. It turned out to be most useful helping soldiers on the ground in New Guinea and other Pacific areas.
funFacts: The prototype made its first flight from Fishermans Bend in Melbourne on 29 May 1942, flown by CAC test pilot Ken Frewin.
It borrowed parts and ideas from the CAC Wirraway trainer to speed up the design.
Before the Boomerang, fighter aircraft had never been built in Australia.
Boomerangs could be a handful on landing because they were prone to ground looping, which means swerving sharply sideways on the runway.
spotterTips: A short, chunky single-seat fighter with a big round radial engine and a large three-blade propeller. It looks a bit like a stubby Wirraway with a single-seat canopy.

melbourne.where: Designed and built by CAC at Fishermans Bend. The RAAF Museum at Point Cook displays Boomerang A46-30, and the Australian National Aviation Museum at Moorabbin has Boomerang A46-25. A flying Boomerang from the RAAF heritage fleet has appeared at the Avalon airshow.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force squadrons in Australia and the Pacific.

name: Avro Lancaster
engines: 4 × Rolls-Royce Merlin XX V12 piston engines
crew: 7 (pilot, flight engineer, navigator, bomb aimer, wireless operator and 2 gunners)
summary: The Lancaster was Britain's most successful heavy bomber of the Second World War, with a huge bomb bay and four Merlin engines. Many Australians flew in Lancasters, and one RAAF Lancaster called G for George is a treasured exhibit in Canberra.
funFacts: Specially modified Lancasters of No. 617 Squadron carried Barnes Wallis's 'bouncing bomb' for the famous Dambusters raid in 1943.
The bomb aimers on that raid used a simple wooden triangle with a peephole and two nails as a sight.
Some Lancasters were modified to carry the 22,000 lb Grand Slam, one of the heaviest bombs of the war.
Only two Lancasters can still fly today, one in Britain and one in Canada.
spotterTips: A big mid-wing bomber with four engines, a glazed nose turret and twin oval tail fins at the ends of the tailplane.

melbourne.where: Lancaster G for George, flown by No. 460 Squadron RAAF, is on display at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra.
melbourne.operators: RAAF squadrons in RAF Bomber Command, such as No. 460 Squadron, and thousands of Australian aircrew.

photo.file: Battle of Britain Memorial flight Avro Lancaster (cropped).jpg

name: Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress
engines: 4 × Wright R-1820-97 Cyclone turbosupercharged radial piston engines
summary: The B-17 Flying Fortress was a four-engine American bomber that flew mostly daytime missions over Europe in the Second World War. It was famous for being tough and able to bring its crews home even after heavy damage.
funFacts: A newspaper reporter invented the name Flying Fortress in 1935 after seeing all the gun positions sticking out of the prototype.
Its crew of 10 included a gunner who rode in a ball-shaped turret hanging under the belly.
As of October 2025 only three B-17s were still in flying condition, with about 50 more in museums or storage.
The oldest surviving B-17, called The Swoose, flew in the Pacific on the first day the United States entered the war.
spotterTips: A four-engine bomber with a very tall, curved tail fin, a glass nose with a chin turret on the G model, and lots of gun positions along the body.

name: Consolidated PBY Catalina
role: Flying boat and amphibian for patrol, search and rescue
engines: 2 × Pratt & Whitney R-1830-92 Twin Wasp 14-cylinder radial piston engines
summary: The Catalina is a flying boat that can land on water, and the amphibian versions can land on runways too. It flew long patrols over the oceans in the Second World War, rescued many airmen from the sea, and was very important to the RAAF and Qantas.
funFacts: From 1943 to 1945 Qantas flew Catalinas non-stop between Perth and Colombo, flights so long that passengers saw the sun rise twice. They were called the Double Sunrise flights.
US Navy Catalinas used for night missions in the Pacific were painted black and nicknamed Black Cats.
In 1941 an RAF Catalina found the German battleship Bismarck far out in the Atlantic.
In 1951 Sir Gordon Taylor flew an ex-RAAF Catalina called Frigate Bird II from Australia to Chile, the first flight across the South Pacific in that direction.
spotterTips: A boat-shaped hull hanging below a huge wing mounted on a pylon, with two engines on the wing and floats that fold up to become the wingtips. Big blister windows on the sides near the tail.

melbourne.where: The Australian National Aviation Museum at Moorabbin has Catalina A24-88, the RAAF Museum at Point Cook displays a Catalina, and the Flying Boat Museum at Lake Boga near Swan Hill displays Catalina A24-30 next to a wartime communications bunker.
melbourne.operators: RAAF squadrons Nos. 11, 20, 42 and 43, and Qantas Empire Airways. Lake Boga was a wartime RAAF flying boat repair base.

name: Messerschmitt Me 262
summary: The Me 262 was the world's first operational jet-powered fighter, used by Germany late in the Second World War. It was much faster than the propeller fighters of its day and showed that jets were the future of air combat.
funFacts: It first flew in 1941 with a propeller engine in the nose because the jet engines were not ready yet. Its first flight on jet power alone came on 18 July 1942.
Fighter versions were nicknamed Schwalbe, meaning Swallow, and fighter-bomber versions Sturmvogel, meaning Storm Bird.
Its Jumo 004B jet engines needed an overhaul after just 25 hours, and 35 hours was the absolute limit for the turbine.
Flying reproductions were built in the United States in the 2000s, using modern General Electric engines.
spotterTips: A sleek fighter with a triangular-section fuselage, swept-back wings and two long jet engines slung under the wings.

photo.file: Messerschmitt Me 262A at the National Museum of the USAF (cropped).jpg

name: Lockheed Super Constellation
engines: 4 × Wright R-3350 Duplex-Cyclone turbo-compound radial piston engines
crew: 5 (pilot, copilot, navigator, flight engineer and radio operator)
summary: The Super Constellation was a stretched version of Lockheed's elegant Constellation airliner, flying long routes across oceans in the 1950s before jets took over. Qantas flew them, and one is still flying in Australia today.
funFacts: It entered service with Eastern Air Lines in December 1951, flying between Miami and New York.
The last Constellation of any kind was built in 1959, a Super Constellation freighter for the Flying Tiger Line.
Each Wright Turbo-Compound engine could make about 3,250 horsepower for take-off.
The Historical Aircraft Restoration Society's Super Constellation VH-EAG received an Engineering Heritage Marker from Engineers Australia.
spotterTips: Look for the triple tail, a long curving fuselage that droops at the nose and four big radial engines. Wingtip fuel tanks were an option on later versions.

melbourne.where: HARS's airworthy Super Constellation VH-EAG is based at Shellharbour Airport (Albion Park) in New South Wales and has visited airshows around Australia.
melbourne.operators: Qantas flew Super Constellations from 1956. VH-EAG is flown by the Historical Aircraft Restoration Society.

photo.file: Lockheed L1049C CF-TGC TCA LAP 12.09.54 edited-2.jpg

name: de Havilland Comet
crew: 4 (2 pilots, flight engineer and radio operator or navigator)
summary: The Comet was the world's first jet airliner, first flying in 1949 and carrying paying passengers from 1952. Early Comets suffered accidents caused by metal fatigue, and the lessons learnt made every later airliner safer.
funFacts: Investigators tested a whole Comet fuselage by pressurising it over and over in a water tank to find out why the early accidents happened.
Its four jet engines were tucked inside the roots of the wings rather than hanging underneath.
The Comet was later turned into the Hawker Siddeley Nimrod maritime patrol aircraft, which served with the RAF until 2011, more than 60 years after the Comet first flew.
The last Comet flight was made by Comet 4C Canopus on 14 March 1997.
spotterTips: A sleek four-jet airliner with the engines buried in the wing roots and a rounded nose. It has a pressurised cabin with a row of large windows.

melbourne.where: Qantas studied the Comet closely in the early 1950s and later leased Comet 4s from the British airline BOAC.
melbourne.operators: Qantas (leased from BOAC).

photo.file: BEA de Havilland DH-106 Comet 4B Berlin.jpg

name: Boeing 707
summary: The Boeing 707 was the jet airliner that made international jet travel normal in the late 1950s and 1960s. Qantas was the first airline outside the United States to fly it, bringing the jet age to Australia in 1959.
funFacts: Boeing test pilot Tex Johnston rolled the 707 prototype upside down in a barrel roll over Lake Washington in Seattle in 1955.
Qantas ordered a special shorter version, the 707-138, so it could fly the long routes it needed.
VH-XBA, one of the first Qantas 707s and the first civilian jet registered in Australia, is on display at the Qantas Founders Museum in Longreach, Queensland.
Special versions of the 707 served as Air Force One for United States presidents.
spotterTips: A four-engine jet with swept wings, engines hanging on pylons under the wings and a thin spike-like antenna on top of the tail fin on many airframes.

melbourne.where: Qantas Founders Museum in Longreach, Queensland, displays VH-XBA. An ex-Qantas 707 donated by actor John Travolta reached the Historical Aircraft Restoration Society in New South Wales in 2026.
melbourne.operators: Qantas from 1959, and later the Royal Australian Air Force.

name: Concorde
manufacturer: British Aircraft Corporation and Sud Aviation
engines: 4 × Rolls-Royce/Snecma Olympus 593 Mk 610 turbojet engines with afterburners
summary: Concorde was a supersonic airliner that flew passengers at about twice the speed of sound, crossing the Atlantic in around three and a half hours. British Airways and Air France flew it from 1976 until 2003, and no passenger jet since has matched it.
funFacts: Its fastest Atlantic crossing, New York to London in February 1996, took just 2 hours, 52 minutes and 59 seconds.
It was painted a special bright white to stop its aluminium skin overheating from air friction at Mach 2.
Its long pointed nose drooped down for take-off and landing so the pilots could see the runway.
In 1992 an Air France Concorde flew around the world in under 33 hours.
spotterTips: A slender white jet with a huge triangular delta wing, no separate tailplane, a long pointed nose that can droop, and four engines in two pairs under the wings.

melbourne.where: Concorde visited Australia on special charter flights, such as a British Airways flight from Christchurch to Sydney in April 1989. Qantas once held options to buy Concorde but never took any.
melbourne.operators: British Airways and Air France only.

name: Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird
engines: 2 × Pratt & Whitney J58 afterburning turbojet engines
